claim: The study screened 613 additional genes using the C. elegans mechanosensory neuron axotomy model.
source: We screened 613 additional genes representing nine classes of protein function and structure, selected based on their sequence conservation and the availability of viable genetic mutants with normal axon development (Figure 1A,B; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of genes screened and the model used.

claim: From the 613 genes screened, 49 genes were identified as promoting PLM regrowth (showing reduced regrowth in loss-of-function mutants).
source: From these 613 genes, we identified 49 genes promoting PLM regrowth (i.e. showing reduced regrowth in loss-of-function mutants) and 34 genes inhibiting regrowth (i.e. increased regrowth in loss-of-function mutants) (Tables 1 and 2; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly reports the number of genes identified with specific phenotypes from the screen.

claim: From the 613 genes screened, 34 genes were identified as inhibiting regrowth (showing increased regrowth in loss-of-function mutants).
source: From these 613 genes, we identified 49 genes promoting PLM regrowth (i.e. showing reduced regrowth in loss-of-function mutants) and 34 genes inhibiting regrowth (i.e. increased regrowth in loss-of-function mutants) (Tables 1 and 2; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript directly reports the number of genes identified with specific phenotypes from the screen.

claim: NMAT-2/NMNAT, a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) synthesizing enzyme, has an unexpected role in axon regeneration.
source: We identify an unexpected role of the nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) synthesizing enzyme, NMAT-2/NMNAT, in axon regeneration.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a finding of the study.

claim: NMAT-2 inhibits axon regrowth via cell-autonomous and non-autonomous mechanisms.
source: NMAT-2 inhibits axon regrowth via cell-autonomous and non-autonomous mechanisms.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding.

claim: NMAT-2 enzymatic activity is required to repress regrowth.
source: NMAT-2 enzymatic activity is required to repress regrowth.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding.

claim: The percentage of genes having positive or negative effects on regrowth was similar to that reported in the previous screen (Chen et al., 2011).
source: The percentage of genes having positive or negative effects on regrowth was similar to that reported in our previous screen (Chen et al., 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting this screen remains far from saturated.
evidence: The manuscript compares the current screen results to a previous study and references a figure showing this comparison.

claim: The combined analyses of >1200 genes reinforce the conclusion that regenerative axon regrowth requires many genetic pathways.
source: The combined analyses of >1200 genes reinforce the conclusion that regenerative axon regrowth requires many genetic pathways, most of which are not involved in developmental axon outgrowth or guidance.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes findings from multiple screens to draw this conclusion.

claim: Most genetic pathways involved in regenerative axon regrowth are not involved in developmental axon outgrowth or guidance.
source: The combined analyses of >1200 genes reinforce the conclusion that regenerative axon regrowth requires many genetic pathways, most of which are not involved in developmental axon outgrowth or guidance.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the combined screen data.

claim: PLM regrowth was enhanced in two independent nmat-2 null mutants, tm2905 and ju1512.
source: We found that PLM regrowth was enhanced in two independent nmat-2 null (0) mutants, tm2905 and ju1512 (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results showing enhanced regrowth in specific mutants.

claim: A null mutation of NMAT-1, a close paralog of NMAT-2, did not affect PLM regrowth.
source: A null mutation of NMAT-1, a close paralog, did not affect PLM regrowth (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for NMAT-1 mutants.

claim: nmat-2(0) adult animals are sterile.
source: nmat-2(0) adult animals are sterile, while nmat-1(0) are fertile, indicating that these two NMNATs may have distinct tissue- or cell-type-specific roles.
evidence: The manuscript reports observed phenotypes of the mutants.

claim: nmat-1(0) animals are fertile.
source: nmat-2(0) adult animals are sterile, while nmat-1(0) are fertile, indicating that these two NMNATs may have distinct tissue- or cell-type-specific roles.
evidence: The manuscript reports observed phenotypes of the mutants.

claim: NMAT-2 and NMAT-1 may have distinct tissue- or cell-type-specific roles.
source: nmat-2(0) adult animals are sterile, while nmat-1(0) are fertile, indicating that these two NMNATs may have distinct tissue- or cell-type-specific roles.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the differential phenotypes observed.

claim: Among enzymes in the NAD+ salvage pathway, only qns-1(0) mutants showed marginally increased axon regrowth.
source: Among these, only qns-1(0) mutants showed marginally increased axon regrowth (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for multiple enzymes in the pathway.

claim: NMAT-2 and QNS-1 catalyze the terminal steps of the NAD+ salvage pathway.
source: NMAT-2 and QNS-1 catalyze the terminal steps of the NAD+ salvage pathway.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established biochemical knowledge.

claim: qns-1(0) mutants are sterile.
source: Like nmat-2(0), qns-1(0) mutants are sterile (Wang et al., 2015) (this work), while other single mutants are fertile, suggesting that NMAT-2 and QNS-1 define essential steps in the biosynthesis of NAD+.
evidence: The manuscript reports observed phenotypes with citation to prior work and current observations.

claim: Neither wild type nor nmat-1(0) grown in FUdR showed increased PLM regrowth.
source: To address whether sterility of the animals might contribute to the observed effects on axon regrowth, we cultured animals on 5'fluoro-2' deoxyuridine (FUdR) and found that neither wild type or nmat-1(0) grown in FUdR showed increased PLM regrowth (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from FUdR treatment experiments.

claim: Sterile animals following germline ablation do not affect PLM regrowth.
source: Additionally, we have previously reported that sterile animals following germline ablation do not affect PLM regrowth (Kim et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work.

claim: NMAT-2's role in axon regrowth is independent of animal fertility.
source: Thus, we conclude that NMAT-2's role in axon regrowth is independent of animal fertility.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the FUdR and germline ablation experiments.

claim: A single copy transgene expressing nmat-2(+) under its endogenous promoter (juSi347) fully rescued the sterility of nmat-2(0).
source: Using CRISPR genome editing, we generated a single copy transgene expressing nmat-2(+) under its endogenous promoter (juSi347). This transgene fully rescued the sterility of nmat-2(0) and restored the increased axon regrowth in nmat-2(0) mutants to wild-type levels (Figure 2C), confirming that the increased axon regrowth is due to loss of NMAT-2 function.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from rescue experiments.

claim: The juSi347 transgene restored the increased axon regrowth in nmat-2(0) mutants to wild-type levels.
source: Using CRISPR genome editing, we generated a single copy transgene expressing nmat-2(+) under its endogenous promoter (juSi347). This transgene fully rescued the sterility of nmat-2(0) and restored the increased axon regrowth in nmat-2(0) mutants to wild-type levels (Figure 2C), confirming that the increased axon regrowth is due to loss of NMAT-2 function.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from rescue experiments.

claim: The increased axon regrowth in nmat-2(0) mutants is due to loss of NMAT-2 function.
source: This transgene fully rescued the sterility of nmat-2(0) and restored the increased axon regrowth in nmat-2(0) mutants to wild-type levels (Figure 2C), confirming that the increased axon regrowth is due to loss of NMAT-2 function.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the rescue experiment results.

claim: Transgenic expression of NMAT-2 in individual tissues (epidermis, intestine, or mechanosensory neurons) was not able to restore axon regeneration in nmat-2(0) to normal.
source: Transgenic expression of NMAT-2 in individual tissues was not able to restore axon regeneration in nmat-2(0) to normal (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: The combined expression of NMAT-2 in all three tissues (epidermis, intestine, and mechanosensory neurons) restored normal axon regeneration.
source: Interestingly, the combined expression of NMAT-2 in all three tissues restored normal axon regeneration (Figure 2D), and also partially rescued sterility.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from multi-tissue rescue experiments.

claim: The combined expression of NMAT-2 in all three tissues partially rescued sterility.
source: Interestingly, the combined expression of NMAT-2 in all three tissues restored normal axon regeneration (Figure 2D), and also partially rescued sterility.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from multi-tissue rescue experiments.

claim: NMAT-2 may act in both neuronal and non-neuronal cells to inhibit axon regeneration.
source: We conclude that NMAT-2 may act in both neuronal and non-neuronal cells to inhibit axon regeneration.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: Several NMNAT proteins function as molecular chaperones, including Drosophila NMNAT, mouse NMNAT2, and human NMNAT3.
source: In addition to their enzymatic roles, several NMNAT proteins function as molecular chaperones, including Drosophila NMNAT, mouse NMNAT2, and human NMNAT3 (Ali et al., 2016; Zhai et al., 2006; Zhai et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on NMNAT protein functions.

claim: The nmat-2(ju1514) mutant with a mutation in the active site motif involved in ATP recognition displayed sterility and enhanced regrowth of PLM neurons.
source: Using CRISPR genome editing, we mutated the active site motif involved in ATP recognition (Zhang et al., 2002) (Figure 2B). This mutant nmat-2(ju1514) displayed sterility and enhanced regrowth of PLM neurons (Figure 2C), indistinguishable from nmat-2(0) mutants.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from the active site mutant.

claim: The role of NMAT-2 in axon regeneration likely requires its enzymatic activity.
source: Therefore, the role of NMAT-2 in axon regeneration likely requires its enzymatic activity.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the active site mutant results.

claim: The enhanced axon regeneration in nmat-2(0) reflects sustained low levels of NAD+.
source: Here, we infer that the enhanced axon regeneration in nmat-2(0) reflects sustained low levels of NAD+.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this as an inference from the data.

claim: The neuroprotective effect of NMNAT is cell-autonomous in Drosophila and in mice.
source: The neuroprotective effect of NMNAT is cell-autonomous in Drosophila and in mice (Gilley et al., 2013; Wen et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on NMNAT neuroprotection.

claim: NMNAT may function via distinct mechanisms for neuroprotection vs. axon regeneration.
source: Our finding that NMAT-2 inhibits axon regrowth via several tissues suggests that NMNAT may function via distinct mechanisms for neuroprotection vs. axon regeneration.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from comparing their findings to prior work on neuroprotection.

claim: In Drosophila, lack of NMNAT led to enhanced sensory axon regeneration.
source: In Drosophila, lack of NMNAT also led to enhanced sensory axon regeneration (Chen et al., 2016b).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on Drosophila NMNAT.

claim: There are conserved roles of NMNAT in axon regeneration.
source: Together, these data suggest conserved roles of NMNAT in axon regeneration.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from comparing C. elegans and Drosophila findings.

claim: JPH-1 is the sole Junctophilin in C. elegans.
source: JPH-1 is the sole Junctophilin in C. elegans (Yoshida et al., 2001) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript states this with citation to prior work.

claim: jph-1(ok2823) mutants exhibited a significantly increased rate of reconnection or fusion between the regrowing axon and distal fragment.
source: We observed that jph-1(ok2823) mutants, likely null, exhibited a significantly increased rate of reconnection or fusion between the regrowing axon and distal fragment (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for jph-1 mutants.

claim: Axons that did not reconnect in jph-1 mutants exhibited reduced axon regeneration, compared to controls.
source: Axons that did not reconnect in jph-1 mutants exhibited reduced axon regeneration, compared to controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for jph-1 mutants.

claim: Axon-axon fusion requires the fusogen EFF-1.
source: Axon-axon fusion requires the fusogen EFF-1 (Ghosh-Roy et al., 2010; Pérez-Vargas et al., 2014) and a phosphoserine-mediated apoptotic cell engulfment pathway (Neumann et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on axon fusion mechanisms.

claim: Axon-axon fusion requires a phosphoserine-mediated apoptotic cell engulfment pathway.
source: Axon-axon fusion requires the fusogen EFF-1 (Ghosh-Roy et al., 2010; Pérez-Vargas et al., 2014) and a phosphoserine-mediated apoptotic cell engulfment pathway (Neumann et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on axon fusion mechanisms.

claim: The enhanced reconnection in jph-1 mutants was greatly reduced in eff-1; jph-1 double mutants.
source: We analyzed eff-1; jph-1 double mutants and found that the enhanced reconnection in jph-1 was greatly reduced (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from double mutant analysis.

claim: JPH-1-mediated contacts may restrict axon-axon fusion, dependent on eff-1.
source: These observations suggest JPH-1-mediated contacts may restrict axon-axon fusion, dependent on eff-1.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the double mutant analysis.

claim: ESYT-2 is the sole E-Syt in C. elegans and is most closely related to human E-Syt2 and E-Syt3.
source: ESYT-2 is the sole E-Syt in C. elegans and is most closely related to human E-Syt2 and E-Syt3 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The manuscript states this based on sequence analysis.

claim: esyt-2 showed wide expression in the nervous system.
source: We found that esyt-2 showed wide expression in the nervous system (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports expression pattern observations.

claim: In the mechanosensory neuron cell body, full-length GFP-ESYT-2 showed a punctate pattern, colocalizing with an ER marker PISY-1 at the peripheral ER.
source: In the mechanosensory neuron cell body, full-length GFP-ESYT-2 showed a punctate pattern, colocalizing with an ER marker PISY-1 (Rolls et al., 2002) at the peripheral ER (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript reports microscopy observations with citation for the ER marker.

claim: In uninjured axons, ESYT-2 was distributed intermittently.
source: In uninjured axons, ESYT-2 was distributed intermittently (Figure 3F; upper panel).
evidence: The manuscript reports microscopy observations.

claim: Upon axon injury, axonal ESYT-2 condensed into small puncta almost immediately (<1 s).
source: Strikingly, upon axon injury, axonal ESYT-2 condensed into small puncta almost immediately (<1 s) (Figure 3F; lower panel).
evidence: The manuscript reports microscopy observations of injury response.

claim: The injury-induced Ca2+ transient triggers ESYT-2 relocalization to axonal ER-PM contact sites.
source: As axon injury triggers a rapid rise in axonal calcium (Ghosh-Roy et al., 2010), we speculate that the injury-induced Ca2+ transient triggers ESYT-2 relocalization to axonal ER-PM contact sites.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this as speculation based on prior work and their observations.

claim: Vertebrate E-Syt1 can localize to ER-PM contact sites following an increase in cytosolic calcium.
source: This is consistent with the observation that vertebrate E-Syt1 can localize to ER-PM contact sites following an increase in cytosolic calcium (Giordano et al., 2013; Idevall-Hagren et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior published work on vertebrate E-Syt1.

claim: esyt-2 null mutant animals were indistinguishable from wild-type animals in growth rate, body morphology, and exhibited normal axon development and regrowth.
source: We generated esyt-2 null mutants by genome editing (Figure 3D). These mutant animals were indistinguishable from wild-type animals in growth rate, body morphology, and exhibited normal axon development and regrowth (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports phenotypic observations of esyt-2 mutants.

claim: ESYT-2 does not appear to be essential for axon regrowth.
source: Thus, while ESYT-2 undergoes temporal changes in response to axon injury, it does not appear to be essential for axon regrowth.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the esyt-2 mutant phenotype.

claim: Loss of function in anoh-1 or anoh-2, or the anoh-1; anoh-2 double mutant, did not affect PLM axon regeneration.
source: However, we found that loss of function in anoh-1 or anoh-2, or the anoh-1; anoh-2 double mutant, did not affect PLM axon regeneration (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for anoctamin mutants.

claim: Each obr single mutant displayed normal regeneration.
source: Each obr single mutant displayed normal regeneration, and the quadruple mutant displayed a significant decrease in axon regrowth (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for OSBP-related protein mutants.

claim: The obr quadruple mutant displayed a significant decrease in axon regrowth.
source: Each obr single mutant displayed normal regeneration, and the quadruple mutant displayed a significant decrease in axon regrowth (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for OSBP-related protein mutants.

claim: Single mutants for all genes in the neutral lipolysis pathway showed no detectable effects in PLM axon regrowth.
source: We tested single mutants for all these genes and double or triple mutants for ABHD (α/β hydrolase domain) genes and observed no detectable effects in PLM axon regrowth (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for lipolysis pathway mutants.

claim: Single mutants for all genes involved in lipophagy showed normal PLM regrowth.
source: We found that single mutants for all these genes showed normal PLM regrowth (Figure 4B), suggesting that lipolysis may not play an essential role in PLM axon regeneration.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for lipophagy pathway mutants.

claim: Lipolysis may not play an essential role in PLM axon regeneration.
source: We found that single mutants for all these genes showed normal PLM regrowth (Figure 4B), suggesting that lipolysis may not play an essential role in PLM axon regeneration.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the lipolysis mutant results.

claim: cept-2 null mutants showed a significant reduction in axon regrowth.
source: Of all mutants affecting individual enzymes in the Kennedy pathway, we found that cept-2 null mutants showed a significant reduction in axon regrowth (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for Kennedy pathway mutants.

claim: cept-1; cept-2 double mutants are embryonic or larval lethal.
source: In testing functional redundancy between cept-1 and cept-2, we found double mutants to be embryonic or larval lethal (data not shown), preventing further analysis.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from genetic crosses.

claim: The Kennedy pathway may affect axon regeneration.
source: Overall, our analysis suggests that the Kennedy pathway may affect axon regeneration.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the Kennedy pathway mutant results.

claim: Two independent ivns-1 mutants (gk252 and ok3171) showed increased axon regrowth.
source: We analyzed two independent ivns-1 mutants (gk252 and ok3171) and observed increased axon regrowth, which was restored to control levels following transgenic expression of ivns-1 driven by its own promoter (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for ivns-1 mutants.

claim: Transgenic expression of ivns-1 driven by its own promoter restored increased axon regrowth in ivns-1 mutants to control levels.
source: We analyzed two independent ivns-1 mutants (gk252 and ok3171) and observed increased axon regrowth, which was restored to control levels following transgenic expression of ivns-1 driven by its own promoter (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from rescue experiments.

claim: ivns-1 mutants showed increased regrowth as early as 6 hr post-injury.
source: ivns-1 mutants showed increased regrowth as early as 6 hr post-injury (Figure 5C), while growth cone formation in ivns-1 mutants was normal (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results at early time points.

claim: Growth cone formation in ivns-1 mutants was normal.
source: ivns-1 mutants showed increased regrowth as early as 6 hr post-injury (Figure 5C), while growth cone formation in ivns-1 mutants was normal (Figure 5D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results on growth cone formation.

claim: Mutants in two other BTB-Kelch proteins kel-8 and kel-20 displayed normal regrowth.
source: The effects of ivns-1 on axon regrowth appeared to be unique, as mutants in two other BTB-Kelch proteins kel-8 and kel-20 displayed normal regrowth (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for other BTB-Kelch proteins.

claim: A loss-of-function mutant (gm121) of EPI-1/Laminin α showed enhanced regrowth.
source: We further analyzed mutants of essential BM structural components and found that a loss-of-function mutant (gm121) of EPI-1/Laminin α and a gain-of-function mutant (tk75) of EMB-9/Type IV collagen (Kubota et al., 2012) both showed enhanced regrowth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), supporting defined roles of specific BM components in axon regrowth.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for basement membrane mutants.

claim: A gain-of-function mutant (tk75) of EMB-9/Type IV collagen showed enhanced regrowth.
source: We further analyzed mutants of essential BM structural components and found that a loss-of-function mutant (gm121) of EPI-1/Laminin α and a gain-of-function mutant (tk75) of EMB-9/Type IV collagen (Kubota et al., 2012) both showed enhanced regrowth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), supporting defined roles of specific BM components in axon regrowth.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for basement membrane mutants with citation.

claim: ADT-1 and ADT-3 promote PLM axon regrowth.
source: We tested null mutants in all five ADAMTS homologs and found that ADT-1 and ADT-3 promote and MIG-17 inhibits PLM axon regrowth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for ADAMTS mutants.

claim: MIG-17 inhibits PLM axon regrowth.
source: We tested null mutants in all five ADAMTS homologs and found that ADT-1 and ADT-3 promote and MIG-17 inhibits PLM axon regrowth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for ADAMTS mutants.

claim: RAB-8 was required for PLM axon regrowth.
source: We found that RAB-8 was required for PLM axon regrowth, whereas RAB-11.2 showed no impact (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that post-Golgi vesicle trafficking, rather than endosome recycling, may be important for axon regrowth.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for Rab GTPase mutants.

claim: RAB-11.2 showed no impact on PLM axon regrowth.
source: We found that RAB-8 was required for PLM axon regrowth, whereas RAB-11.2 showed no impact (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that post-Golgi vesicle trafficking, rather than endosome recycling, may be important for axon regrowth.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for Rab GTPase mutants.

claim: Post-Golgi vesicle trafficking, rather than endosome recycling, may be important for axon regrowth.
source: We found that RAB-8 was required for PLM axon regrowth, whereas RAB-11.2 showed no impact (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that post-Golgi vesicle trafficking, rather than endosome recycling, may be important for axon regrowth.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the Rab GTPase mutant results.

claim: NEX-1 and NEX-2 have an inhibitory role on PLM regrowth.
source: We found that NEX-1 and NEX-2 have an inhibitory role on PLM regrowth, whereas NEX-3 and NEX-4 have no impact (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for Annexin mutants.

claim: NEX-3 and NEX-4 have no impact on PLM regrowth.
source: We found that NEX-1 and NEX-2 have an inhibitory role on PLM regrowth, whereas NEX-3 and NEX-4 have no impact (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for Annexin mutants.

claim: MEC-17, but not ATAT-2, was required for normal axon regrowth.
source: Here, we tested two α-tubulin acetyltransferases, MEC-17 and ATAT-2, which acetylate the α-tubulin MEC-12 that is enriched in mechanosensory neurons (Akella et al., 2010). We found that MEC-17, but not ATAT-2, was required for normal axon regrowth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for tubulin acetyltransferase mutants with citation.

claim: mec-17; atat-2 double mutants showed reduced axon regrowth resembling the mec-17 single mutant.
source: mec-17; atat-2 double mutants showed reduced axon regrowth resembling the mec-17 single mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that MEC-17-dependent acetylated MTs are permissive for axon regrowth.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for double mutants.

claim: MEC-17-dependent acetylated MTs are permissive for axon regrowth.
source: mec-17; atat-2 double mutants showed reduced axon regrowth resembling the mec-17 single mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), suggesting that MEC-17-dependent acetylated MTs are permissive for axon regrowth.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the double mutant results.

claim: Loss of function in mec-12 or tba-9 resulted in reduced regrowth.
source: We found that loss of function in mec-12 or tba-9 resulted in reduced regrowth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for tubulin isotype mutants.

claim: Loss of function in tba-7 showed enhanced regrowth.
source: In contrast, loss of function in tba-7 showed enhanced regrowth.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for tubulin isotype mutants.

claim: TBA-7/α-tubulin likely functions as a destabilizing factor for MTs.
source: A recent study that examined the neurite growth of mechanosensory neurons has proposed that TBA-7/ α -tubulin likely functions as a destabilizing factor for MTs (Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a recent study proposing this function.

claim: Partial loss-of-function mutants of fli-1 displayed reduced PLM axon regrowth.
source: Of the three Gelsolin-related proteins in C. elegans, gsnl-1 and viln-1 null mutants showed normal regrowth while partial loss-of-function mutants of fli-1 displayed reduced PLM axon regrowth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for Gelsolin-related protein mutants.

claim: Lack of the Twinfilin homolog TWF-2 increased axon regrowth.
source: In contrast, lack of the Twinfilin homolog TWF-2 increased axon regrowth.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for Twinfilin mutants.

claim: Loss-of-function mutation in tmc-1 results in enhanced regeneration.
source: We found several new genes in which loss-of-function mutation results in enhanced regeneration, including the sodium-sensitive channel tmc-1 (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2013) and an acetylcholine receptor alpha subunit (CHRNA6) lgc-12 (Cohen et al., 2014) (Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for channel mutants with citations.

claim: Loss-of-function mutation in lgc-12 results in enhanced regeneration.
source: We found several new genes in which loss-of-function mutation results in enhanced regeneration, including the sodium-sensitive channel tmc-1 (Chatzigeorgiou et al., 2013) and an acetylcholine receptor alpha subunit (CHRNA6) lgc-12 (Cohen et al., 2014) (Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for channel mutants with citations.

claim: MFSD-6 promotes PLM regrowth.
source: Additionally, we found that MFSD-6, a member of the Major Facilitator Superfamily Domain (MFSD) family, promotes PLM regrowth (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for MFSD-6 mutants.

claim: Loss-of-function mutants of mfsd-6 exhibited reduced axon regrowth, which was rescued by expressing wild type mfsd-6 under a pan-neuronal promoter.
source: Loss-of-function mutants of mfsd-6 exhibited reduced axon regrowth, which was rescued by expressing wild type mfsd-6 under a pan-neuronal promoter (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results for MFSD-6 mutants and rescue experiments.

claim: The frequency of axon regrowth phenotypes may be consistent across screening platforms.
source: Interestingly, a recent genome-wide screen for enhanced regrowth in mouse cortical neurons reported a positive hit rate of 3% (Sekine et al., 2018), whereas we find 3.9% of genes displayed significantly elevated axon regrowth. The frequency of axon regrowth phenotypes may therefore be consistent across screening platforms.
evidence: The manuscript compares their hit rate to a published mouse screen and draws this conclusion.

claim: PLM axons were severed ~50 μm distal from the cell body in the fourth larval (L4) stage using a femtosecond laser.
source: In the PLM axon regrowth model, we sever the axon ~50 μm distal from the cell body in the fourth larval (L4) stage using a femtosecond laser and measure axon regrowth 24 hr post-axotomy in at least 10 animals per strain (Wu et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental method with citation.

claim: Axon regrowth was measured 24 hr post-axotomy in at least 10 animals per strain.
source: In the PLM axon regrowth model, we sever the axon ~50 μm distal from the cell body in the fourth larval (L4) stage using a femtosecond laser and measure axon regrowth 24 hr post-axotomy in at least 10 animals per strain (Wu et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental method with citation.

claim: Genes affecting axon regrowth are found across all functional and structural classes tested.
source: As in our previous screen, genes affecting axon regrowth are found across all functional and structural classes tested (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the distribution of hits across gene classes.

claim: This screen remains far from saturated.
source: The percentage of genes having positive or negative effects on regrowth was similar to that reported in our previous screen (Chen et al., 2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting this screen remains far from saturated.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from comparing hit rates between screens.

claim: Axon regeneration after injury is an important and conserved biological process in many animals.
source: Axon regeneration after injury is an important and conserved biological process in many animals, involving a large number of genes and pathways (He and Jin, 2016; Mahar and Cavalli, 2018; Tedeschi and Bradke, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Upon axonal injury, distal axon segments degenerate and segments proximal to the cell body remain alive and can in certain cases regenerate.
source: Upon axonal injury, distal axon segments degenerate and segments proximal to the cell body remain alive and can in certain cases regenerate (Chen et al., 2007; McQuarrie and Grafstein, 1973; Neumann and Woolf, 1999).
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge with citations.

claim: Axon regeneration after injury requires rapid sealing of the damaged plasma membrane and subsequent formation of growth cones.
source: Axon regeneration after injury requires rapid sealing of the damaged plasma membrane (PM) and subsequent formation of growth cones, leading to regrowth and extension from damaged proximal axons.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge.

claim: Calcium entry via voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the PM is critical for PLM axon regeneration.
